title: Spatially informed demand-side policies for green hydrogen diffusion in Europe - Nature Energy
gist: Using an installation-level diffusion model calibrated on natural gas power plants and an original database of 14,108 prospective European hydrogen offtakers, the study finds that spatial spillovers — local adoption raising nearby adoption probability — are a strong secondary driver of green hydrogen uptake whose effect rises more than twentyfold when hydrogen is far from cost parity. Spillover potential concentrates in a handful of Belgian and German industrial regions and in chemicals and iron and steel, yet EU hydrogen valleys, REPowerEU corridors and European Hydrogen Bank auctions are largely blind to it; targeting the 10% most central offtakers cuts policy cost per additional kilogram of hydrogen demand by 37–41%.

themes.theme: The green hydrogen implementation gap in hard numbers

insights.claim: By the end of 2023 less than 1% of EU hydrogen production came from clean sources and fewer than 7% of global capacity announcements had been completed on schedule, despite the EU and 18 of its 27 member states having adopted green hydrogen strategies.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The gap between announced hydrogen pipelines and delivered projects is roughly an order of magnitude, so headline capacity announcements are a poor basis for underwriting hydrogen offtake or equipment demand.
insights.quote: by the end of 2023, less than 1% of EU hydrogen production originated from clean sources
insights.locator: Main, opening paragraph

insights.claim: Under a mean-cost, central-saturation scenario with carbon pricing but no additional policy support, modelled European green hydrogen demand reaches only about 3 Mt by 2030 — an 83% shortfall against the EU's 20 Mt target — and about 29 Mt by 2050, a 43% shortfall against the 50 Mt implied target.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Baseline demand falls so far below stated EU targets that anyone sizing electrolyser or hydrogen infrastructure markets off official targets is overestimating by a factor of several.
insights.quote: In the mean cost + central saturation scenario, diffusion barely takes off until 2030, with an expected demand of approximately 3 Mt (83% shortfall).
insights.locator: Baseline projections of green hydrogen demand (Fig. 5)

insights.claim: Of nine combinations of cost trajectory and sectoral saturation modelled for Europe, only the single most optimistic pairing — progressive cost decline plus extended saturation into power and heat — reaches the 20 Mt 2030 demand target.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Hitting the 2030 target requires both aggressive cost declines and hydrogen winning in sectors where electrification is usually cheaper — a compound bet, not a base case.
insights.quote: Of all scenario combinations, only the most optimistic (progressive cost + extended saturation) meets the EU’s 2030 target of 20 Mt green hydrogen demand
insights.locator: Baseline projections, Fig. 5b discussion

insights.claim: Reaching the EU's 2030 hydrogen demand target under central saturation assumptions would require green hydrogen costs of €71 MWh−1, some 58% below the study's mean cost trajectory.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It puts a concrete price stake in the ground for what cost level would make policy targets self-fulfilling, and shows how far current expected costs sit from it.
insights.quote: achieving 2030 targets is consistent with green hydrogen costs of €71 MWh−1 (58% below the mean cost trajectory
insights.locator: Baseline projections, carbon pricing discussion

insights.claim: Holding carbon prices constant instead of letting them escalate almost entirely suppresses modelled green hydrogen diffusion through 2050.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The entire baseline hydrogen demand case rests on an escalating EU carbon price; any political softening of carbon pricing would gut the demand thesis before subsidies are even considered.
insights.quote: holding carbon prices constant almost entirely suppresses diffusion through 2050
insights.locator: Baseline projections, carbon price assumptions

themes.theme: Spatial spillovers as a conditional diffusion driver

insights.claim: In a logistic adoption model calibrated on European natural gas power plants, cost competitiveness has an average marginal effect of 14.5 percentage points per standard deviation versus 1.7 points for spatial spillovers — spillovers matter, but cost is roughly eight times larger on average.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It calibrates expectations: geography-aware policy is a meaningful add-on, not a substitute for closing the cost gap.
insights.quote: Cost competitiveness has the largest influence (14.5 percentage points (pp) per s.d., 33% relative to average adoption probability), roughly eight times that of spatial spillovers (1.7 pp per s.d., 4%).
insights.locator: Cost competitiveness and spatial spillovers in diffusion, Fig. 2a

insights.claim: The effect of spatial spillovers on adoption probability rises more than twentyfold above its average when cost competitiveness is in the bottom decile (a cost gap of about −€210 MWh−1) and local diffusion is already high.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Peer and infrastructure effects are most valuable precisely in the early, uneconomic phase where subsidy money is being spent, inverting the intuition that spillovers only matter once a technology is cheap.
insights.quote: When cost competitiveness is very low (lower than the tenth percentile, −€210 MWh−1) and local diffusion is high (near full diffusion), spillover effects increase more than 20-fold.
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion

insights.claim: Spillover effects become immaterial once cost competitiveness rises beyond the 75th percentile, so the policy window for exploiting them closes as the technology approaches cost parity.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Spatially targeted support has a time-limited value window: deploy it while hydrogen is expensive or lose the leverage entirely.
insights.quote: beyond the 75th percentile, become immaterial
insights.locator: Fig. 2c discussion of marginal effects

insights.claim: Distance to navigable waterways and to natural gas transmission pipelines had negligible and statistically insignificant effects on adoption — below 0.3 percentage points — implying that interdependencies between offtakers matter more than static physical geography.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Proximity to existing pipeline routes is a weaker predictor of adoption than clustering with other adopters, which argues against infrastructure-first siting logic.
insights.quote: indicating that offtaker interdependencies matter more than physical geography
insights.locator: Cost competitiveness and spatial spillovers in diffusion, Fig. 2a

insights.claim: Replacing the study's residual-based cost proxy with external levelized cost of electricity data increases the relative importance of spatial spillovers versus cost competitiveness, suggesting the headline estimate of spillover strength is conservative.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Robustness checks lean in favour of the spillover thesis rather than against it, strengthening the case for spatially informed policy.
insights.quote: Replacing the empirical cost proxy with external levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) measures43 yields consistent results, increasing the relative importance of spillovers versus cost competitiveness
insights.locator: Cost competitiveness and spatial spillovers in diffusion

themes.theme: Where the spillover potential actually sits: five regions, two sectors

insights.claim: More than half of the offtakers in the top decile of degree centrality across Europe sit in just five of 243 regions: Antwerp and East Flanders in Belgium and Düsseldorf, Cologne and Rheinhessen-Pfalz in Germany.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Europe's hydrogen demand network is extraordinarily concentrated, so a handful of Belgian and German industrial clusters will determine whether a European hydrogen economy forms at all.
insights.quote: half of the offtakers in the highest centrality decile are located in only 5 out of 243 regions in Belgium (Antwerp and East Flanders) and Germany (Düsseldorf, Cologne and Rheinhessen-Pfalz)
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, Fig. 3a

insights.claim: Corridor potential, measured by betweenness centrality, runs from the North Sea through Germany and Austria toward southeastern Europe with additional signals in coastal Spain and Italy, adding Lombardy, Emilia-Romagna, Münster, Arnsberg, Hainaut and Western Flanders to the high-potential set.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It gives a concrete, named map of where hydrogen transport links would connect the most mutually reinforcing demand, useful for judging which corridor proposals have underlying demand logic.
insights.quote: half of the offtakers in the highest centrality deciles are located in 11 regions
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, Fig. 3b

insights.claim: In the chemicals and iron and steel sectors, 40% of offtakers fall into the top decile of betweenness centrality, versus the 10% that would be expected if influence were evenly spread.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Two sectors hold four times their proportional share of network influence, making them the highest-leverage targets for any demand-side hydrogen instrument.
insights.quote: in the chemicals and iron and steel sectors, 40% of offtakers fall into the top decile of centrality
insights.locator: Fig. 4c, sectoral distribution of betweenness centrality

insights.claim: For local clustering potential, about one-quarter of offtakers in chemicals and shipping and about one-fifth in non-ferrous metals fall into the top centrality decile, indicating heavy-tailed sectoral distributions rather than uniform influence.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Within each priority sector only a minority of sites are network-critical, so screening at installation rather than sector level changes which projects deserve support.
insights.quote: about one-quarter in chemicals and shipping and about one-fifth in non-ferrous metals fall into the top decile of centrality
insights.locator: Fig. 4b discussion

insights.claim: Named installations sitting at the peaks of the European spillover distribution include the ThyssenKrupp steel plants in Duisburg, the INEOS and Evonik chemical sites in the Ruhr valley, and Eni's Sannazaro refinery south of Milan.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It names specific corporate assets whose hydrogen switching decisions would propagate furthest through Europe's prospective demand network.
insights.quote: Prominent installations in these peaks include the ThyssenKrupp steel plants in Duisburg and the INEOS and Evonik chemical sites in the Ruhr valley
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, Fig. 4b

insights.claim: Within North Rhine-Westphalia the most influential offtakers cluster in a 50-km radius between Düsseldorf and Dortmund, and a separate corridor links non-metallic mineral plants at Brno and Zlín through the Vienna Basin to the Leoben metallurgical cluster and Graz in Styria.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The analysis resolves down to specific sub-regional links, showing that useful hydrogen corridors may be far shorter and more local than headline import-corridor plans.
insights.quote: a link extending from Brno and Zlín (non-metallic mineral plants) through the Vienna Basin to industrial centres (Leoben metallurgical cluster, Graz) in Austria’s Styria region
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, Fig. 3c,d

themes.theme: EU policy instruments are misaligned with demand geography

insights.claim: Across all 22 designated EU hydrogen valleys, targeted demand amounts to only 0.2 Mt — equivalent to roughly 1% of the EU's 2030 hydrogen goal — while European Hydrogen Bank auctions disregard demand entirely.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The EU's flagship place-based hydrogen policy is demand-trivial by construction, which explains why supply-side subsidies keep failing to convert into offtake.
insights.quote: EHB auctions disregard demand. For EU hydrogen valleys, the link is weak: across all 22 valleys, targeted demand amounts to only 0.2 Mt
insights.locator: Main, policy under-representation paragraph

insights.claim: With the exception of Northern Italy, EU-designated hydrogen valleys lie outside the areas with the strongest modelled spatial spillover potential.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Public money for regional hydrogen ecosystems is being placed where self-reinforcing adoption is least likely, a direct efficiency loss that a selection-criteria change could reverse.
insights.quote: with few exceptions (Northern Italy), EU-designated valleys lie outside the areas with the strongest spatial spillover potential
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, place-based policy discussion

insights.claim: The three REPowerEU import corridors — North Sea, Mediterranean and Ukraine, operationalized as five subcorridors in the European Hydrogen Backbone plan — are not inconsistent with observed spillover patterns but are too broad and extend far beyond the high-potential regions.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Corridor planning currently spreads capital across geographies with no demand anchor, raising the odds of stranded pipeline assets.
insights.quote: these corridors are broad and could be refined through an explicit link to spillover potential
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, RePowerEU discussion

insights.claim: Prioritizing high-spillover industrial links in hydrogen infrastructure plans would improve investment targeting and reduce future underutilization — explicitly framed as asset stranding risk — of the hydrogen grid.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Stranding risk on hydrogen transmission assets is a live investment concern, and demand-network centrality offers a screening tool for it.
insights.quote: Prioritizing high-spillover industrial links could improve investment targeting and reduce future underutilization (asset stranding risk) of the hydrogen grid.
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, place-based policy implications

insights.claim: The high-spillover regions identified — the Rhine-Ruhr valley, North Sea coast and Southern Poland — overlap with areas supported by the EU's €19.7 billion Just Transition Mechanism, aligning hydrogen targeting with existing regional development funding.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: There is an existing multi-billion-euro funding channel whose geography already matches the hydrogen demand map, creating a politically easier route to co-financing.
insights.quote: key areas (the Rhine-Ruhr valley, North Sea coast and Southern Poland) overlap with regions supported by the EU’s €19.7 billion Just Transition Mechanism
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, regional development alignment

themes.theme: Quantified payoff from spatially targeted subsidy design

insights.claim: Awarding contracts for difference to the 10% most central offtakers, while controlling for sector, cost and installation size, reduces the median policy cost per additional kilogram of green hydrogen demand by 37–41%, or €0.83–0.96 per kilogram, relative to a spatially neutral allocation.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A pure change in who gets the subsidy — no extra budget — buys nearly 40% more demand per euro, which is a rare free lunch in energy policy.
insights.quote: By 2100, spatially informed interventions reduce the median cost per additional kilogramme of green hydrogen demand by 37–41% (€0.83–0.96 kg−1) relative to spatially neutral interventions.
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, Fig. 6e

insights.claim: Adding a spillover-centrality criterion weighted at just 10% to a European Hydrogen Bank-style auction improves cost-effectiveness by 13–15% (€0.17–0.20 per kilogram) and raises 2100 annual demand by up to 1.6%, capturing 20–25% of the fully controlled targeting effect.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The gain survives inside a realistic auction rule, so the recommendation is an incremental tweak to an existing instrument rather than a redesign requiring new legislation.
insights.quote: The amendment increases annual demand in 2100 by up to 1.6% (0.6 Mt; Fig. 6e) and improves cost-effectiveness by 13–15% (€0.17–0.20 kg−1
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, EHB-style auction

insights.claim: Weighting the centrality criterion above 20% in an auction backfires because cost competitiveness losses then outweigh spillover gains, so the optimum is to adjust rather than replace cost-based award rules.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It bounds the policy recommendation quantitatively and preempts the obvious overcorrection of turning auctions into regional-industrial-policy vehicles.
insights.quote: cost competitiveness losses outweigh spillover gains when increasing the centrality criterion’s weight beyond 20%
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, auction weighting

insights.claim: Spatially targeted intervention raises annual 2100 green hydrogen demand by roughly 6–10% (2.2–4.1 Mt) versus the neutral approach, partly because high-centrality offtakers happen to have greater long-run demand potential even after stratifying by size.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Part of the gain comes from composition — targeting influence also selects bigger long-run consumers — which compounds the spillover benefit.
insights.quote: spatially informed interventions increase annual green hydrogen demand (in 2100) by about 6–10% (2.2–4.1 Mt; Fig. 6c)
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, controlled setting

insights.claim: The cost-effectiveness advantage of spatial targeting only emerges from 2040 onwards, because demand differences appear early when costs are high and push up expenditure before spillovers materialize.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Politically, the policy looks more expensive before it looks cheaper, so it requires committed multi-decade support to pay off.
insights.quote: Policy effectiveness advantages emerge from 2040 onwards
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, Fig. 6e

insights.claim: Sustaining these benefits requires policy commitment into the growth and slowdown phases of diffusion, phases in which solar and wind support policies have historically come under political pressure.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The historical record of renewables subsidies being cut mid-diffusion is the main political risk to this policy design.
insights.quote: These benefits materialize over time, requiring sustained policy commitment into the growth and slowdown phases of diffusion, where solar and wind policies have come under pressure
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, supply-side extension argument

themes.theme: Offtake risk and why auction awards do not become plants

insights.claim: The 2025 European Hydrogen Bank auction allocated only €270 million — 20% of the available budget — illustrating that supply-side, minimum-subsidy auction design is failing to clear amid demand uncertainty.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Budget headroom is not the binding constraint on European hydrogen; credible offtake is, which shifts where policy and private capital should be aimed.
insights.quote: its 2025 iteration resulted in only €270 million of allocations—20% of the available budget
insights.locator: Main, policy design paragraph

insights.claim: Auction awards do not necessarily convert into deployment, as shown by the 2.4-GW Hornsea 4 offshore wind project being halted despite holding a £59 MWh−1 contract for difference.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A contracted strike price is not a completion guarantee, so awarded-capacity statistics overstate real pipelines in both wind and hydrogen.
insights.quote: In offshore wind, the 2.4-GW Hornsea 4 project was halted despite a £59 MWh−1 CfD.
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, offtake risk

insights.claim: Ørsted cancelled its 70-MW FlagshipONE e-methanol project two years into construction for lack of viable offtake agreements, incurring a €190 million impairment loss.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A concrete, sizable write-down shows offtake risk is already destroying capital in e-fuels, not just delaying it.
insights.quote: Ørsted’s 70-MW FlagshipONE e-methanol project was cancelled 2 years into construction owing to a lack of viable offtake agreements, incurring a €190-million impairment loss
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, offtake risk

insights.claim: European Hydrogen Bank results show median subsidy needs differ between transport and industry at €1.8 versus €2 per kilogram, which the authors read as room for sector-differentiated targeting rather than a single uniform clearing price.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Uniform auctions leave allocational precision on the table when sectoral subsidy requirements visibly diverge.
insights.quote: EHB results indicate differences in median subsidy needs for transport and industry (€1.8 kg−1 versus €2 kg−1)
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, demand-side instruments

insights.claim: Spillovers crowd in private investment by increasing adoption at nearby sites that receive no direct policy support, which is the mechanism by which targeted subsidies become cheaper per unit of induced demand.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It identifies the specific leverage mechanism — untargeted neighbouring adoption — that investors should look for when judging whether a subsidised cluster will grow organically.
insights.quote: Spillovers further crowd in private investment by increasing nearby adoption without direct policy support.
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, demand-side instruments

themes.theme: Method: natural gas as historical analogue and a 14,108-site database

insights.claim: Because green hydrogen lacks reliable historical deployment data and project announcements are overconfident, the diffusion model is calibrated on all EU natural gas power plants deployed between 1961 and February 2026 from the S&P Capital IQ Power Plant database, selected through the SHARD historical-analogue framework.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: Every headline result is conditional on hydrogen diffusing like natural gas power generation, which is the single biggest assumption a reader should stress-test.
insights.quote: The sample includes all natural gas power plants deployed in the EU between 1961 and February 2026 as recorded in the S&P Capital IQ Power Plant database.
insights.locator: Methods, Empirical model

insights.claim: Natural gas was chosen over renewables as the analogue partly because it received limited policy support — €10 billion versus €83 billion for renewables in 2021 before the Ukraine war — giving a cleaner baseline for evaluating policy effects.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The analogue choice is defended on identification grounds, not just physical similarity, which strengthens the causal reading of the policy simulations.
insights.quote: Unlike renewable generation, natural gas receives limited policy support (€10 billion versus €83 billion for renewables in 2021, before the Ukraine war)
insights.locator: Cost competitiveness and spatial spillovers in diffusion, analogue justification

insights.claim: The study builds an original geo-located database of 14,108 prospective EU offtakers spanning industry, power, heating, airports, ports and fuel stations, covering roughly 70% of EU emissions and all industrial installations emitting more than 25 kt CO2 annually, published openly via GitHub and Zenodo.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: An open, installation-level European decarbonization asset map is reusable well beyond hydrogen, including for CCUS and electrification screening.
insights.quote: the database covers about 70% of EU emissions and all industrial installations emitting more than 25 kt CO2 annually
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential; Data availability

insights.claim: Passenger vehicles and railways are deliberately excluded from the offtaker universe because alternatives are clearly economically or technologically superior there.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The authors treat hydrogen-for-cars as settled and lost, narrowing the credible hydrogen demand story to hard-to-abate industry and select transport modes.
insights.quote: We exclude applications such as passenger vehicles and railways that are unlikely to see material hydrogen adoption, given the clear economic or technological superiority of alternatives
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, database construction

insights.claim: Spillover potential is operationalized with two network centrality metrics on a proximity graph — degree centrality standing in for hydrogen valleys (local influence) and betweenness centrality for hydrogen corridors (mediating influence between otherwise disconnected regions).
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: It supplies a concrete, reproducible screening metric that policymakers or investors could apply to any candidate site list.
insights.quote: degree centrality, indicating hydrogen valleys (local spillovers via direct neighbours) and betweenness centrality, which quantifies the role of offtakers in mediating hydrogen corridors between otherwise disconnected regions
insights.locator: Regions and sectors with spatial spillover potential, network approach

insights.claim: Cost competitiveness is measured with a residual-based latent proxy from a first-pass logit, a technique the authors acknowledge is only valid if the latent signal dominates the residuals, and which correlates 0.7 (R2 of 0.47) with an external natural gas versus coal LCOE spread.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The central explanatory variable is inferred rather than observed, which is the methodological soft spot a sceptical reader should weigh against the strong headline effects.
insights.quote: the LCOE measure is highly related to our proxy (correlation coefficient of 0.7 and R2 of 0.47)
insights.locator: Methods, Empirical model; Limitations

insights.claim: The spatial spillover index is the weighted adoption status of neighbouring installations within a 120-km radius, demeaned cross-sectionally, with the radius chosen by hyperparameter optimization maximizing area under the ROC curve.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The 120-km scale defines what counts as a hydrogen cluster in practice, a concrete planning radius for valley and corridor design.
insights.quote: We calculate this as the weighted adoption status of neighbouring installations within a 120-km radius, which is then demeaned cross-sectionally.
insights.locator: Methods, Empirical model

insights.claim: Competition from electrification, CCUS and biomass is handled through sector-level saturation rates that cap hydrogen adoption, and lower saturation rates also weaken spatial spillovers because less local diffusion means less spillover pressure.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: If hydrogen loses ground to electrification in any sector, the spillover engine weakens too, making the downside case for hydrogen self-reinforcing in the wrong direction.
insights.quote: Lower saturation rates also weaken spatial spillovers because lower local diffusion reduces spillover pressure.
insights.locator: Spatial spillover potential for informing hydrogen policy, uncertainty matrix

insights.claim: The modelling framework is presented as transferable to other technologies shaped by spatial spillovers, explicitly naming carbon capture, utilization and storage and CO2 networks.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The same location-screening logic could reshape how CO2 transport and storage subsidies are allocated, a second policy market for the method.
insights.quote: provide a platform transferable to other technologies shaped by spatial spillovers, such as CCUS and CO2 networks
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, contributions

insights.claim: A shift toward renewable-based production could reorganize global trade and the footprint of energy-intensive production, and EU efforts such as the Clean Industrial Deal Industrial Accelerator Act point toward preserving existing industrial networks rather than letting them relocate.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
entities: Clean Industrial Deal Industrial Accelerator Act
insights.so_what: Whether Europe retains energy-intensive industry at all determines whether the demand network modelled here exists to be subsidised.
insights.quote: Recent EU industrial policy efforts such as the Clean Industrial Deal Industrial Accelerator Act point towards an effort to preserving existing industrial networks
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, trade and industrial footprint

insights.claim: Integrating the European Hydrogen Bank's transparency mechanism, which matches hydrogen supply projects with potential offtakers, into the auction system itself is proposed as a practical way to strengthen demand linkages.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost administrative reform that could raise bid-to-contract conversion without new money.
insights.quote: Integrating the EHB’s transparency mechanism, which matches hydrogen supply projects with potential offtakers, into EHB auction systems could help strengthen demand linkages.
insights.locator: Discussion and conclusion, supply-side extension

insights.claim: The authors argue that integrated assessment models and energy system models such as PRIMES, on which EU climate policy including Fit for 55 relies, cannot deliver the sectoral detail and spatial resolution needed for spatially informed hydrogen policymaking.
insights.speaker: Nature Energy
insights.so_what: The modelling stack underpinning EU climate policy is structurally incapable of seeing the demand-side geography this paper says is decisive.
insights.quote: By representing complex feedback loops between energy and other economic and environmental sectors, IAMs are well positioned to analyse system-level green hydrogen pathways but struggle to represent the sectoral detail and spatial resolution required for spatially informed policymaking
insights.locator: Main, modelling gap paragraph
